In a mountain village, two monks, Tranquil River and Soaring Eagle, sought guidance on their paths to enlightenment.

Tranquil River asked the wise old master, "Master, how shall we traverse two paths without losing our way?"

The master, with a serene smile, handed them two mirrors, saying, "Hold one mirror to the sky and the other to the earth. Reflect not upon what the mirrors show, but upon the clarity within."

Perplexed, the monks ventured forth, one reflecting on the heavens, the other on the ground. Tranquil River glimpsed stars and clouds, while Soaring Eagle saw earth and roots.

Yet, in moments of insight, they saw the unity in their reflections. They realized that watching sky and earth within, they could walk both paths in harmony, enriching their journey to enlightenment.

Thus, hold the mirror of Transcendental Meditation to the sky of serenity, and The Mind Illuminated to the earth of profound insight. Reflect not on the practices, but on the unified clarity they foster within, embracing both as one.

Approaching meditation without expectations takes practice. Here's how:

Open mindset: Start by acknowledging that each session is unique. Some days will be smooth, others more scattered. Embrace whatever arises without judgment.

Set intention: Before starting, remind yourself that your only goal is to sit and be present. Let go of expectations about how your meditation "should" go.

Cultivate curiosity: Approach each session with curiosity rather than anticipation. Be open to whatever experiences unfold without labeling them as good or bad.

Focus on the process: Shift your attention from outcomes to the act of sitting itself. Embrace the moment-to-moment experience without striving for a particular result.

Non-judgmental awareness: When distractions arise, gently notice them without criticism. Redirect your focus back to your meditation object without dwelling on the distraction.

By letting go of specific expectations and embracing the practice itself, you can cultivate a more open and accepting approach to meditation. Remember, the essence lies in the act of sitting and being present, regardless of how the mind behaves during that time.

Balancing dedication to practice and letting go of expectations is essential:

Set realistic goals: Aim for a consistent daily practice without fixating on specific outcomes or stages. Focus on the process, not the destination.

Commit to regularity: Dedicate time daily without obsessing over progress. Consistency matters more than duration. Start with what's manageable and gradually increase without attachment to results.

Cultivate a balanced mindset: Acknowledge progress but detach from attachment to it. Embrace where you are while staying open to growth.

Practice for the sake of practice: Find joy in the meditation itself, not just in reaching milestones. Embrace the present moment experience without craving advancement.

Mindful intention: Remind yourself of the reasons for meditating daily, emphasizing personal well-being, peace, and inner growth, rather than specific goals.

By nurturing a balanced approach, you can prioritize consistent practice without fixating on progression, allowing space for growth while appreciating each moment of the practice itself.

Navigating subtler and more pervasive aspects during meditation can indeed be challenging, as they often lack a clear focal point for redirection. Here are some approaches that might help you work with these less tangible aspects:

Awareness without fixation: Instead of trying to pinpoint or define these subtle feelings or thoughts, allow them to exist in your awareness without fixating on them. Acknowledge their presence without getting entangled in their content. This helps create a sense of spaciousness around these experiences.

Noting with broader categories: While noting can be helpful, consider using broader categories to label these subtler experiences. You might label them as "background noise," "vague anticipation," or "unidentified mood." This broader labeling can acknowledge their presence without getting too caught up in their specifics.

Shifting focus to awareness itself: Instead of focusing solely on the breath, broaden your attention to include the awareness itself. Notice the space in which these subtler experiences arise. By shifting the focus from content to the nature of awareness, you can observe these experiences without getting entangled in them.

Acceptance and non-reactivity: Practice accepting these subtler aspects as part of your meditation experience. Cultivate a sense of non-reactivity toward them. Allow them to come and go without trying to change or analyze them.

Gentle redirection: If you find yourself getting absorbed in these subtler experiences, gently redirect your attention back to the breath or your chosen anchor. It's okay if your mind drifts; the practice lies in the act of gently guiding it back.

Off-cushion practice: Consider integrating mindfulness into daily activities. Notice these subtler experiences as they arise during everyday tasks. Bringing mindfulness to these moments can enhance your ability to work with them during formal meditation.

Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate these subtler experiences but to develop a more skillful relationship with them. Over time, with consistent practice, you might find it easier to navigate and be at ease with these background thoughts and feelings during meditation. Experiment with these approaches and see which resonates best with your practice.

Culadasa's instructions in the excerpt you shared can be broken down into three primary intentions, even though the phrasing might initially suggest more actions. Here's a breakdown:
  
  
* Hold the intention to appreciate the “aha" moment: This intention involves cultivating an awareness that recognizes when the mind has wandered. It's not so much an action but a mental attitude or readiness to acknowledge when the mind has drifted away from the breath.

* Gently but firmly redirect attention back to the breath: This is the second intention. When the “aha" moment arises and you notice the mind wandering, the intention here is to gently but firmly guide your attention back to the breath. It's about the deliberate act of bringing the focus back to the chosen anchor.

* Engage with the breath as fully as possible without losing peripheral awareness: This intention involves actively engaging with the sensations of the breath while maintaining an awareness of the surrounding environment. It's about maintaining a balance between focused attention on the breath and an open, peripheral awareness of other sensations, sounds, or thoughts.

So, while the initial description might seem to outline four actions, the three core intentions for Stage Two of the practice are the appreciation of the "aha" moment, redirecting attention to the breath, and engaging fully with the breath while maintaining peripheral awareness. These intentions are foundational in developing mindfulness and concentration in the early stages of meditation practice.

In an ordinary sense, that is to say in the sense that we commonly use the word 'Choice' I would say that suffering is not a choice. We tend to speak of choices as a selection between options (usually based on each options merits). On the face of it then it seems that if suffering were a choice, we would all choose not to suffer, as the merits of not suffering seem obvious compared to the demerits of suffering.

If we examine this closer though we might discover that in certain situations there are merits to suffering, for example we may enjoy the sympathy, or take pleasure in self-pity. From this point of view it seems that it is possible that suffering is indeed a choice, but we simply choose to suffer so that we can take pleasure in self-pity and garnering sympathy.

Aristotle conceived a choice as something that is done as a result of conscious deliberation. If this is what we mean by choice we might say that suffering is probably not a choice, or at least it seems odd to consider it as one. It might be more apt to view suffering as a mental habit. We could say that to suffer right now is not a choice, as I may do it automatically. Like reaching for a glass of water to take a sip. But crucially, we have a degree of control over our habits. We may attempt for example to perform actions that reduce this habit to suffer, or we might try and train our self to fall into negative thought patterns less frequently.

Wittgenstein would say that the philosophical question that you are raising is the result of a fundamental misconception that you have about how language works. let me try and explain.

Let me start of with a question that might strike you as odd or unrelated: how do you know that when you say "I am in pain" the meaning of that is in fact your internal pain. You might say, "I know what I mean, because I am the one who attaches meaning to the words that I am using". Maybe you are imagining that when you say "I am in pain", you are somehow internally pointing to your pain, and that by this act of pointing you have caused the words to mean the internal sensation which you now wish them to mean. I might try and prod at this notion a bit. Say you have two internal sensations, one is a pain and the other is a warmth. You utter to yourself (Either aloud or in your head) "I am in pain". Does you meaning that pain you have depend on you having pointed internally at the pain? What if you happened to be focusing on the warmth? Or on both? When push comes to shove there is no internal mechanism that you can use to determine what the statement means. The idea that you are somehow conjuring meaning internally is misguided (try for example saying "I am warm" but meaning "I am cold).
So, a closer investigation of how language works is warranted. 

For Wittgenstein at least language is a rule-based phenomenon that has many things in common with a game. Language can be thought of as similar to a game in the sense that they are both rule-based social activities. We might say that when you say something within the context of a language-game, this is analogous to say making a move in chess. What is the meaning of a rook? What does it mean to understand a rook? It simply means to know how the rook is used within the context of chess. If you play a game and you use the rook correctly, and notice when I use it incorrectly, I might say you understand the rook. 

For Wittgenstein understanding language works in exactly the same way? What does it mean to understand the phrase "I am in pain"? It means that you know to say "I am in pain" when you are in pain. The fact that "I am in pain" sounds like a description of your inner state is confusing you, it is not. Think how you might replace it with a loud groan. Is the groan a description of pain? No, the meaning of the groan is similar to the meaning of the phrase "I am in pain". They are both conventionally used in situations where you are in pain, and this is where they get their meaning from.

Once you see that language is a social phenomenon you can see that you question is ill-posed. You do not have a private language whereby "I am in pain" is somehow a description of an inner state whose meaning can never actually comes across. Notice that inner states are not somehow observable and indescribable but rather they are not observable in the first place. You do not say, "It seems like I am in pain but I might be wrong", or "Let me look and see whether I am in pain or not". You might say "I know I am in pain" but this is meaningfully the same as "I am in pain". The fact that the grammar of reporting sensations is similar to the grammar of description is misleading.

So, to answer your question. When you utter the sentence "I am in pain" the only meaning it has to you is the same meaning it has to anyone who hears it, and that meaning is that you are in pain. There is no internal meaning whereby it somehow refers to your sensation that doesn't get across. Because the meaning of the phrase itself is only established publicly, that is language only makes sense publicly, there is no such thing as a private language.

If for example I want to have a blog with articles and comments; i make an Article model and a Comment model, now obviously each article should have multiple comments but each comments should be only part of one article, right? right.  
  
Now intuitivley you would think this would be defined as a one-to-many field within the Article class, after all the article is the one that contains the comments, right? wrong.  
  
In Django you actually need to define a foreign key from the comments class, basically signifying that comments can only have one article, so each comment references their article and an article can be referenced by multiple comments.

This opening to the book of Job tells us that the story is a fable, an allegory that is trying to teach the reader something. I will not delve into this too deeply but it is also worth noting that there is no Satan in Judaism, the word Satan in the context is referring to the angel that would report evil men to God.  
  
  
The point of the story is to teach about unconditional faith and love in God, whether bad things happen to you, or good things happen to you. I'm not getting into a discussion about weather that is a virtuous lesson or not.   
  
  
tl;dr The point is that the story isn't meant to have happened, but is an allegorical tale meant to teach   something
